newsitem.title: POLAND: Growing Polish domestic demand inflates C/A gap.
newsitem.headline: Growing Polish domestic demand inflates C/A gap.

text.p: Poland's current account deficit boomed in the first quarter of 1997 as exports grew slowly amid a flood of imports created by growing domestic demand for investment and consumer goods.

The National Bank of Poland said earlier on Tuesday that Poland's current account deficit amounted to $355 million in March and $1.487 billion in the first quarter, against a C/A surplus of $151 million in the same period of 1996.

"It is not surprising that Poland has such a C/A deficit as its economy is growing at around seven percent, while demand for investment is more than (year-on-year) 20 percent," said Krzysztof Bledowski, chief economist at WoodCommerz in Warsaw.

Exports grew just 4.1 percent in the first quarter while imports jumped 26.6 percent, which widened Poland's merchandise trade deficit to $3.07 billion in the January-March period from a $1.44 billion shortfall in the same period of 1996.
Cross-border inflows shrank by a third to $1.22 billion in the first quarter, as smaller price differentials and a weak German mark discouraged many would be cross-border shoppers.

"Poland's trade gap is still not large in GDP terms when compared to other central European countries, but as cross border trade inflows slow the deficit is bound to rise," said Jacek Kuczynski, analyst at PBR SA.
Analysts had said that Poland's trade deficit may grow to $11-12 billion in 1997 from $8.15 billion last year.

"Such a deficit could be in the works even if exports start to pick up in the third or fourth quarter as traders begin to reap profits from the zloty's fall against the dollar and from the better economic climate in Germany as well as other European Union countries," Bledowski said.
The zloty has weakened nearly 10 percent in nominal terms against the dollar from the start of the year, while holding nearly flat against the mark, as the German unit remained weak on world markets.

Official currency reserves remained flat in the first quarter, ending March at $17.98 billion, just $56 million less than in December 1996, despite a nearly $1.5 billion debt buy-back by the Polish government over the last several months.
